title: Why Distance Two Is Exceptional for Poisson–Binomial Point Probabilities

paper.title: Why Distance Two Is Exceptional for Poisson–Binomial Point Probabilities
paper.abstract:
Abstract Let S S be a finite sum of independent Bernoulli random variables. We ask
how large the mean must be before the atom at k + r k+r can strictly exceed the
atom at k k . For the threshold T k , r := inf { \E ​ S : \Pp ​ ( S = k + r ) > \Pp ​ ( S = k ) } T_{k,r}:=\inf\{\E S:\Pp(S=k+r)>\Pp(S=k)\} , the adjacent case recovers the
classical Darroch boundary k + 1 / ( k + 2 ) k+1/(k+2) , while every gap r ≥ 3 r\geq 3 has threshold k + 1 k+1 . Distance two is the unique nonadjacent exception: T k , 2 = k + Δ k T_{k,2}=k+\Delta_{k} ,
where Δ k \Delta_{k} and its staircase optimizer are explicit and Δ k = 1 / 2 + 1 / 2 ​ k − 1 / ( 4 k ) + O ( k − 3 / 2 ) \Delta_{k}=1/2+1/\sqrt{2k}-1/(4k)+O(k^{-3/2}) . The proof combines the
classical fixed-mean reduction to shifted binomial laws with an exact discrete
optimization. The result also yields sharp restrictions on nonadjacent
coefficient reversals in real-rooted polynomials with nonnegative
coefficients.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Knowing the mean of a count is much easier than knowing its whole distribution. But what does the mean tell us about two individual probabilities? Let S = X 1 + ⋯ + X n , X i ∼ Bernoulli ⁡ ( p i ) , S=X_{1}+\cdots+X_{n},\qquad X_{i}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_{i}), where the summands are independent and 0 ≤ p i ≤ 1 0\leq p_{i}\leq 1 . Fix integers k ≥ 0 k\geq 0 and r ≥ 1 r\geq 1 . We ask how large \E ​ S \E S must be before \Pp ​ ( S = k + r ) \Pp(S=k+r) can exceed \Pp ​ ( S = k ) \Pp(S=k) . More precisely, define T k , r := inf { \E ​ S : \Pp ​ ( S = k + r ) > \Pp ​ ( S = k ) } , T_{k,r}:=\inf\bigl\{\E S:\Pp(S=k+r)>\Pp(S=k)\bigr\}, (1) where the infimum ranges over all finite Bernoulli sums, with no prescribed number of summands. Probabilities outside the support are set to zero. The strict comparison excludes ties between two zero masses. The adjacent case belongs to the classical theory of the mode. Darroch [ 1 , Theorem 4] proved that every mode of a Bernoulli sum lies within one unit of its mean and obtained the sharper boundary k + 1 / ( k + 2 ) k+1/(k+2) for a change between k k and k + 1 k+1 . Samuels [ 4 ] studied the successive differences of these distributions. Pitman [ 5 ] presents these results together with their real-rooted polynomial interpretation; his bounds for consecutive coefficient ratios are particularly close to our question. Baker and Handelman [ 7 ] use the ratio of the second-largest to the largest mass of a unimodal law as a measure of local flatness. More recently, Gnedin [ 8 ] studied how cheaply an added Bernoulli or Poisson increment can move the mode. Distance two is linked to this circle of ideas by a one-line identity. If C ∼ Bernoulli ⁡ ( 1 / 2 ) C\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2) is independent of S S , then \Pp ​ ( S + C = k + 2 ) − \Pp ​ ( S + C = k + 1 ) = \Pp ​ ( S = k + 2 ) − \Pp ​ ( S = k ) 2 . \Pp(S+C=k+2)-\Pp(S+C=k+1)=\frac{\Pp(S=k+2)-\Pp(S=k)}{2}. Thus the case r = 2 r=2 asks for the smallest mean of a Bernoulli sum for which a fixed fair coin is critical for moving the mode past k + 1 k+1 . Gnedin fixes the base law and optimizes the increment; here the increment is fixed and the base Bernoulli sum is optimized under a mean constraint. For a nonadjacent pair, a reversal can happen in two ways: the two positive masses can cross, or the support can move past the lower index. These mechanisms behave differently. At distance two and k ≥ 1 k\geq 1 , the crossing comes first and leaves a genuine discrete optimization; at k = 0 k=0 the two boundaries coincide. From distance three onward, the support barrier k + 1 k+1 wins. We evaluate the crossing level exactly and describe all ties at the boundary. The first step is classical. The extremal idea goes back to Tchebichef [ 2 ] ; Hoeffding’s general fixed-mean result [ 3 , Theorem 3] reduces the symmetric multi-affine functional used here to parameters taking only the values 0 0 , 1 1 , and one common interior value. Mattner [ 6 ] gives a modern multi-moment extension. The one-moment argument is short enough to include, after which the problem becomes an explicit discrete optimization. Increasing q k q_{k} gives strict reversal. In every case, \Pp ​ ( S = k + r ) > \Pp ​ ( S = k ) \Pp(S=k+r)>\Pp(S=k) implies \E ​ S > T k , r \E S>T_{k,r} ; the infimum in ( 1 ) is not attained by a strict reversal. The middle line is the part to understand. One might expect the boundary to be reached by k + 2 k+2 trials, as in the adjacent case. sections.text: The fair-coin identity puts the exceptional case directly into the language of mode transport: the distance-two comparison is an adjacent comparison with one success probability fixed at 1 / 2 1/2 . Baker–Handelman’s ratio [ 7 ] records how flat a unimodal peak is, while Gnedin’s peak skewness [ 8 ] records the smallest Bernoulli parameter that moves the leading mode of a fixed base law. Here the perturbing parameter is fixed at 1 / 2 1/2 , and the quantity being minimized is instead the mean of the base Bernoulli sum. At the distance-two boundary the optimizing law has unique mode k + 1 k+1 and equal flanks at k k and k + 2 k+2 . Thus a fair Bernoulli is exactly critical for moving that mode: after convolution, the masses at k + 1 k+1 and k + 2 k+2 tie. In Gnedin’s terminology [ 8 ] , the critical peak skewness is 1 / 2 1/2 . Applying the unrestricted refined Darroch bound to S + C S+C gives only \Pp ​ ( S = k + 2 ) > \Pp ​ ( S = k ) ⟹ \E ​ S > k + 1 2 + 1 k + 3 . \Pp(S=k+2)>\Pp(S=k)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\E S>k+\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{k+3}. Conversely, the finite binomial examples already establish sharpness. Even when λ > 0 \lambda>0 is required, adding an arbitrarily small Poisson component to a strict finite example preserves the reversal by continuity. This extends the thresholds, not the equality classification in Proposition 7 . Remark 10 (A fixed number of trials) . If the number n n of Bernoulli trials is prescribed and zero parameters are allowed, the same thresholds are already available for n ≥ k + 1 n\geq k+1 when r = 1 r=1 , n ≥ k + d k n\geq k+d_{k} when r = 2 r=2 , and n ≥ k + r n\geq k+r when r ≥ 3 r\geq 3 . A first-moment constraint controls the order of two specified atoms, with a binomial crossing at distance two and a support threshold at every larger distance. The exceptional constant records exactly where those two mechanisms part company.

But what does the mean tell us about two individual probabilities? Let S = X 1 + ⋯ + X n , X i ∼ Bernoulli ⁡ ( p i ) , S=X_{1}+\cdots+X_{n},\qquad X_{i}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_{i}), where the summands are independent and 0 ≤ p i ≤ 1 0\leq p_{i}\leq 1 . Probabilities outside the support are set to zero. The strict comparison excludes ties between two zero masses. The adjacent case belongs to the classical theory of the mode. Darroch [ 1 , Theorem 4] proved that every mode of a Bernoulli sum lies within one unit of its mean and obtained the sharper boundary k + 1 / ( k + 2 ) k+1/(k+2) for a change between k k and k + 1 k+1 . Samuels [ 4 ] studied the successive differences of these distributions. Pitman [ 5 ] presents these results together with their real-rooted polynomial interpretation; his bounds for consecutive coefficient ratios are particularly close to our question. Baker and Handelman [ 7 ] use the ratio of the second-largest to the largest mass of a unimodal law as a measure of local flatness. More recently, Gnedin [ 8 ] studied how cheaply an added Bernoulli or Poisson increment can move the mode. Distance two is linked to this circle of ideas by a one-line identity.
